title: “Don’t call me Naomi,” she said. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.” — Ruth 1:20
paragraphs: “Don’t call me Naomi,” she said. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.” — Ruth 1:20
There are moments in Scripture where God allows us to see a wound so deep that most people rush past it because it feels too uncomfortable to examine.
Naomi is one of those wounds.
Most people remember the Book of Ruth as a beautiful love story. Redemption. Restoration. Boaz. The lineage of David. The shadow of Christ.
But hidden beneath the surface is a woman who became spiritually exhausted under the crushing weight of loss.
A woman who no longer recognized herself.
A woman who believed God Himself had turned against her.
And if we are honest, many believers secretly understand Naomi more than they admit.
They still attend church. They still know Scripture. They still speak respectfully about God.
But deep inside, there is bitterness they never healed from.
The Meaning Hidden Inside Naomi’s Name
The root word comes from the Hebrew:
Naomi’s very identity was tied to sweetness.
But by the time we encounter her in Ruth chapter 1, sweetness had been replaced by sorrow.
Al-tiqre’nah li Na‘omi; qre’nah li Mara
“Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara.”
This was identity transformation through suffering.
“The woman you once knew no longer exists.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Naomi did not become bitter overnight.
Bitterness almost never begins with rebellion.
“In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land.”
The Hebrew word for famine is:
There was no bread in the House of Bread.
God intentionally allows that tension to appear in the text.
Sometimes the very place that once fed you becomes the place where you feel empty.
The marriage that once felt alive becomes cold. The ministry that once burned with passion becomes mechanical. The prayer life that once felt intimate becomes silent.
And in desperation, people begin leaving spiritually familiar territory searching for survival.
That is exactly what Naomi’s family did.
Ruth 1:1-2 tells us Naomi’s husband Elimelech took his family to Moab.
Moab was not merely another country.
The Moabites descended from Lot’s incestuous relationship with his daughter in Genesis 19.
Their origins were marked by shame.
Throughout Scripture, Moab often represents compromise, opposition, and spiritual distance from covenant life.
Yet famine drove Naomi’s family there.
Pain has a way of pushing people into places they never thought they would go.
Sometimes suffering does not instantly destroy faith.
Then Naomi’s sons marry Ruth and Orpah.
One woman left standing in silence.
The Hebrew text in Ruth 1:5 says:
There are believers carrying this exact feeling.
People moved on. The world kept spinning. Church services continued. But internally they remained standing beside emotional graves nobody else understood.
And this is where bitterness begins to grow.
But because pain remained unanswered too long.
Naomi says something shocking in Ruth 1:13:
“The hand of the LORD has gone out against me.”
“The hand of Yahweh has come against me.”
“I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.”
אֲנִי מְלֵאָה הָלַכְתִּי וְרֵיקָם הֱשִׁיבַנִי יְהוָה
Ani mele’ah halakhti, vereiqam heshivani YHWH
“Full I departed, but empty Yahweh has returned me.”
She still used His covenant name.
But she interpreted every loss through the lens of divine hostility.
This is one of the most dangerous forms of spiritual bitterness.
A faith that still acknowledges God’s existence while quietly accusing His character.
Many people sitting in churches today are spiritually here.
But internally they carry hidden accusations:
“Why did You allow this?” “Why didn’t You stop it?” “Why did You stay silent?”
God heard every one of those thoughts.
The Difference Between Grief And Bitterness
The Son of God openly entered human sorrow.
The New Testament uses the Greek word:
“Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you.”
Bitterness becomes dangerous because it slowly poisons perception.
A bitter person no longer interprets life clearly.
Naomi could no longer see God’s mercy unfolding beside her.
Ruth was literally standing next to her.
Future redemption was walking beside her.
But bitterness blinded her to hope.
It convinces wounded people that the story already ended.
Ruth — The Grace Naomi Could Not Yet Recognize
One of the most powerful contrasts in the Book of Ruth is that Naomi speaks emptiness while heaven quietly sends provision.
“Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
The Hebrew concept behind Ruth’s devotion connects deeply to:
steadfast love, loyal covenant mercy, faithful lovingkindness.
Even while Naomi believed God had abandoned her, God had already positioned Ruth as part of her restoration.
But Naomi could not yet see it.
Some people are asking God where He is while He is already moving through people, circumstances, warnings, delays, and unseen protection.
Naomi’s Bitterness Was Honest — But Incomplete
This is where careful biblical interpretation matters.
Scripture does not hide her anguish.
The Bible is brutally truthful about human emotion.
She believed the story was over.
This is why temporary pain should never become permanent theology.
A single season cannot fully interpret God’s eternal intentions.
“For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways, declares the LORD.”
Human beings often judge God from unfinished chapters.
The Hidden Prophecy Inside Naomi’s Story
The Book of Ruth eventually reveals Boaz as the kinsman redeemer.
redeemer, restorer, one who rescues family inheritance.
This points directly toward Jesus Christ.
Because humanity also became spiritually empty.
“All we like sheep have gone astray.”
Humanity wandered spiritually far from God.
The Gospel is not merely self-improvement.
The New Testament reveals this through the Greek word:
“[Jesus] gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.”
The cross was not symbolic sentiment.
It was redemption purchased with blood.
Naomi’s story whispers this long before Bethlehem would eventually receive another child — Jesus Christ.
Jesus Himself was born in Bethlehem.
The House of Bread eventually received the Bread of Life.
The Danger Of Secret Bitterness Toward God
Some people do not hate God openly.
Bitterness often disguises itself as disappointment.
“God failed me.” “God abandoned me.” “God took too much.”
“See to it that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble.”
Many people manage symptoms while the root remains alive.
They become cynical. Emotionally detached. Spiritually numb. Unable to celebrate others. Unable to trust God fully.
But here is the terrifying reality.
Naomi no longer wanted to be called Naomi.
And many people have done the same thing internally.
Their betrayal became their identity. Their divorce became their identity. Their addiction became their identity. Their failure became their identity.
But Jesus did not die merely to improve behavior.
Naomi’s Restoration Began Before She Felt It
One of the deepest truths in Ruth is that God was already restoring Naomi before Naomi emotionally recognized restoration.
Because modern culture often treats feelings as ultimate truth.
God’s activity is not dependent upon human emotional awareness.
Even in Naomi’s bitterness, providence was moving.
The Hebrew concept of divine providence silently saturates Ruth.
No miracles split the sea. No fire falls from heaven. No angels visibly appear.
A field. A meeting. A harvest. A redeemer. A lineage. A future King.
Some of God’s greatest works happen silently.
That is why believers must be careful not to interpret silence as absence.
The answer to bitterness is not pretending pain never happened.
The answer is not motivational positivity.
The answer is redemption through Christ.
“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good.”
This does not mean all things are good.
Death is not good. Sin is not good. Betrayal is not good.
But God is powerful enough to redeem what humans cannot repair.
That is the center of Christianity.
Three days later, heaven revealed redemption.
The cross looked like the end.
And some people reading this have been interpreting their lives from Friday while God is still writing Sunday.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
If bitterness is never surrendered, it can harden the soul against the very mercy meant to heal it.
Naomi Eventually Held Redemption In Her Arms
At the end of Ruth, Naomi holds Obed — the grandfather of King David.
“A son has been born to Naomi.”
The woman who called herself empty became part of the lineage leading to Jesus Christ.
God was writing a larger story than Naomi understood.
And He still does that today.
Some people think their suffering disqualified them.
But throughout Scripture, God repeatedly enters broken stories.
Abraham was old. Moses was insecure. David failed. Peter denied Christ. Paul persecuted believers.
Boaz redeemed Ruth and restored Naomi’s household.
Humanity stands guilty before a holy God because of sin.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Sin is not merely bad behavior.
It is rebellion against God’s holiness.
And bitterness itself can become sin when humans place themselves in judgment over God.
But Christ came to rescue sinners.
“For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son.”
Jesus lived the sinless life humanity could not live.
He died on the cross for sinners.
The wrath against sin fell upon Him.
Then He rose again victorious over death.
Some People Are Still Living As Mara
But privately they still call themselves bitter.
They still define themselves by what they lost.
But Christ can restore what bitterness tried to bury.
Not always by recreating the old life.
God never promised believers a painless existence.
“In the world you will have tribulation.”
“Take heart; I have overcome the world.”
The Question Naomi’s Story Leaves Behind
Will pain become your permanent identity?
Or will you allow Christ to redeem even the places that broke you?
Because many people know Scripture intellectually while secretly living emotionally as Mara.
And the terrifying part is that bitterness can survive inside religious language for years.
But Jesus still calls the weary.
Still heals. Still restores. Still redeems.
The cross remains proof that God can bring resurrection out of devastation.
If this pierced something hidden in you, do not ignore it.
Somebody reading this has blamed God for years while still pretending everything is fine.
But His mercy is still reaching for you.
